product.title: Slovak 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Slovak: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Slovak builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the six cases — introduced one at a time, each with an everyday job — to the imperfective and perfective verb pairs that English has no direct equivalent for. Includes a sound chart for all 46 letters, the rhythm rule, a six-case summary, a list of the verbs used in the course, and a glossary.

blocks.text: Slovak is usually introduced with one number that makes people back away at once: **six cases**. Every noun has six forms, and each form changes again depending on the noun's gender. The number is true, and there is no point hiding it.

But that number hides something just as important: Slovak **has no articles**. No *a* and *the*, no *der/die/das*, no *le/la*. *Kniha* means "book", "a book", and "the book" all at once. It feels strange for a week, and then it is pure relief — one whole decision English makes you take in every sentence simply disappears.

The second gift is the spelling. Slovak is written **almost exactly the way it sounds**. Once you know that *č* is *ch*, *š* is *sh*, and *j* is *y*, you can read any word correctly — including words you have never seen. No silent letters, none of the surprises English and French are full of.
The third gift: **stress always falls on the first syllable**. Always, no exceptions, however long the word. One rule, learned once, used for life.

So Slovak's difficulties are real, but they gather in just three places: **six cases** that change the end of a noun, **noun gender**, which decides which ending you use, and **imperfective and perfective verb pairs** — two verbs for one action, which separate "I was writing" from "I wrote it all, to the end".

That is why none of the three is piled up at the front or pushed to the back. The cases come in **one at a time**, one case per unit, each with a clear everyday job: the accusative for ordering in a café (unit 4), the locative for saying where things are (unit 6), the genitive for shopping (unit 9), the dative for saying you like something or that something hurts (unit 10), the instrumental for naming who you are with and what you use (unit 17). The verb pairs get a whole unit of their own in unit 15.
The explanations are short on purpose. What is long is not the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours in scraps. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read aloud. In Slovak this is cheap: the spelling is honest and the stress is always at the front.

From the very first noun, write down its **gender** together with the word — not *stôl*, but *stôl (m)*. You cannot guess its case endings without it. This ten-second habit is what separates the beginner who flows from the one who stumbles.

Don't wait for your pronunciation to be perfect before you dare to speak. Slovaks rarely meet foreigners who bother to learn their language; even a small effort gets a far warmer welcome than you expect.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Veľa šťastia!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place, and the six cases are added one by one from unit 4 to unit 17.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting of about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — read the Slovak aloud first, without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most, yet it is where you see how Slovak *thinks*. Example: *Ako sa voláš?* literally means "how self you-call?", not "what is your name".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt odd a moment ago.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, with their pronunciation and gender.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have really tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. The trick is reversed: cover the Slovak, look at the English, and rebuild the Slovak sentence from memory.
This is the part that turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Each time you meet a new noun, say it three ways in one go: the basic form, the "in" form, and the object form. *škola → v škole → školu*. *obchod → v obchode → obchod*. Ten seconds a word, and the six cases stop being a table to memorize.
When you're unsure which ending to use, don't guess from the meaning — look at **the last letter of the basic form**. The answer is almost always there.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Slovak rewards that generously, because the writing is honest — once you know the chart on the next pages, you can read anything.
This section is short, and that is the good news. Slovak spelling is **almost completely honest**: a letter is always read the same way, in any word. All you need to do is learn the list below once.

The **Say it** column throughout the course uses English-friendly spelling, with capitals marking the stressed syllable. Vowels are always pure: **ah** as in *father*, **eh** as in *bed*, **ee** as in *see*, **oh** as a short, pure *o*, **oo** as in *food*; **ai** as in *eye*, **ay** as in *say*, **ow** as in *how*. Because Slovak stress **always** falls on the first syllable, the capitals are predictable — they stay so your eye gets used to them.
The stress rule: one sentence

**Stress is always on the first syllable.** Always. No matter how long the word: *slo-ven-či-na* → **SLOH**-vehn-chee-nah, *Bra-ti-sla-va* → **BRAH**-tee-slah-vah, *ne-roz-u-miem* → **NEH**-rohz-oo-myehm. This is one of the cheapest rules in any European language — learn it once and never get it wrong again.

blocks.title: One small trap in this easy rule
items: A one-syllable preposition **merges** with the next word and pulls the stress onto itself: *do školy* is said **DOH**-shkoh-lee, not doh-**SHKOH**-lee. The same goes for *na stole*, *v meste*, *za domom*.

Certain short words are **never stressed at all**: *som, si, je, sme, ste, sú, sa, si, mi, ti, ho, ju*. They cling to the word before them like a tail. That's why *volám sa* sounds like one word: **VOH**-lahm-sah.

blocks.text: Watch the pair that gets mixed up most: **c** is read *ts*, while **č** is read *ch*. One small mark above the letter, two very different sounds. *Cena* (price) and *čierna* (black) do not start with the same sound.
Four soft letters: ď, ť, ň, ľ
The ˇ mark over *d, t, n, l* means the tongue presses further forward while adding a little *y* sound. You already know *ň*: it is the *ny* in *canyon*. The other three follow the same pattern.

blocks.title: A free rule: softening that isn't written
items: When *d, t, n, l* meet **e** or **i**, they **soften by themselves** even though the mark isn't written. *deti* is read *DYEH-tyee*, *ticho* is read *TYEE-khoh*, *nie* is read *nyeh*, *leto* is read *LYEH-toh*.
So you rarely need to remember the ˇ — Slovak spelling saves it exactly where it's predictable. The mark is written only when the soft letter meets **a, o, u**, as in *ďakujem* and *ľudia*.
The exceptions: borrowed words (*telefón* = TEH-leh-fohn, not *tyeh-*) and a few words like *ten* (tehn) and *jeden* (YEH-dehn).

blocks.text: Vowels: long and short change the meaning

The acute mark over a vowel (*á, é, í, ó, ú, ý*) is not a stress mark — it means **the vowel is held about twice as long**. The stress stays on the first syllable, even when the long vowel comes later.

head: Letter
Sounds like
Example
rows: short *ee* / long *ee* — **y sounds exactly like i**
short *oh* / long *oh* (*ó* appears almost only in borrowed words)
**eh** — in everyday speech the same as *e*

blocks.text: Four gliding sounds and the letter ô

The letter **ô** looks odd but is easy to say: one syllable that glides from *oo* to *o*, like the start of *water* followed by a pure *o*. *Kôň* = *kwohny* (horse), *môj* = *mwoy* (my), *stôl* = *stwohl* (table).
Words without vowels

Slovak lets **r** and **l** carry a syllable on their own, so some words have no vowel letter at all. They're not as hard as they look: roll the *r* a little longer and let your tongue slip in a faint, quick *uh*. The **Say it** column writes these syllables bare — *krk*, PR-vee, SLN-koh — so you remember not to add a full vowel.

blocks.title: A sentence to test your nerve
items: *Strč prst skrz krk.* — "Stick a finger through your throat." Four words, not one vowel letter. Slovaks use it to test foreigners, and if you can say it, you've made a friend on the spot.
The cheat: **stuhrch puhrst skuhrs kuhrk**. Slip in a faint *uh*, not a full vowel.

blocks.text: The rhythm rule: two longs may not sit side by side

One rule that other European languages don't have, and that explains many odd endings later: **two long syllables may not follow each other in one word**. If the syllable before is already long, an ending that should be long is **shortened**.

head: Base form
Usual long ending
Result
Why
rows: *že-* is short, the ending may be long

blocks.text: This rule is set out fully in unit 7 and used again in unit 18. For now it's enough to know that when you see an ending that "should be long" but is written short, it is **not a typo**.
These pages are not for studying — they're for a quick look when you forget a form in the middle of an exercise. Everything here has already been explained slowly in its own unit.

blocks.text: 2. Singular case endings

Two things that cover most beginner mistakes: **masculine nouns for living beings take the ending *-a* as an object** (*vidím muža*), while things don't change at all (*vidím stôl*). And **feminine nouns ending in *-a* take *-u* as an object** (*mám kávu*) — the ending you'll need most often in this course.
3. Gender: guessing from the last letter
4. byť — to be

Its negative is special and must be learned separately: **nie som, nie si, nie je, nie sme, nie ste, nie sú** — two words, not a prefix. Every other verb uses the joined prefix *ne-*: *nerobím, nemám, nechcem*.
5. Three verb classes
6. Past and future

**Past** = stem + *-l* matching the subject's gender + *som/si/sme/ste*. The third person takes nothing: *robil som* (I, a man, did), *robila som* (I, a woman, did), *robil* (he did). The word *som* almost always sits in **second place** in the sentence: *Včera som bol doma*, not *Včera bol som doma*.

**Future** has two roads. For **imperfective** verbs: *budem* + dictionary form (*budem robiť* = I will be doing). For **perfective** verbs: the present form **already** means future (*urobím* = I'll get it done). This is why unit 15 exists.

blocks.text: The verbs below cover most everyday A1 conversation. They're listed in dictionary form, with the *ja* form in the second column because that's where the class shows. The perfective partner is given where there is one.

If you've reached this page after really working through all twenty units, you have a complete A1: you can introduce yourself, ask the way, order food, go shopping, say what hurts, tell the story of yesterday, and make plans for tomorrow. More importantly, you've got past the barrier that makes many people quit — six cases, noun gender, and perfective verb pairs.
To move on to A2, these three things pay off fastest:

items: **The plural in all six cases.** At A1 you used the plural only in the nominative and genitive. Completing the other four makes your sentences sound grown-up at once, and there are far fewer endings than you fear — many are the same for all three genders.

**Verb prefixes, seriously.** At A1 you used them only to make perfective partners. At A2 you'll find that a prefix can change the meaning completely: *písať* (to write) → *napísať* (to write to the end) → *podpísať* (to sign) → *opísať* (to describe) → *prepísať* (to copy out).

**The conditional (*podmieňovací spôsob*).** The *chcel by som* you've used since unit 16 is actually this form. Completing it — *mohol by som, vedel by som* — instantly makes you sound much more polite.

blocks.text: And one gift waits at the end: Slovak and Czech are **mutually intelligible without extra study**. Slovaks watch Czech films without subtitles, and vice versa. Once you reach A2 in Slovak, you practically get two countries at once — and much of Polish, Ukrainian, Croatian, and Slovenian becomes far easier to read than before. One Slavic language mastered is a door to the next ten.
*Veľa šťastia a dovidenia!*
